statements.quote: The propositions covered mainstream UK political issues balanced across the political spectrum, from healthcare and immigration to climate policy and civil liberties (see SI:2.8 for the full list).
Users edited the AI-generated paragraphs only 23% of the time (<30% across all models and input types at p<.01; see SI:4.1), and most edits were minor (median Levenshtein ratio = 0.96).

Writers reported moderate-to-high engagement with their assigned propositions (median issue knowledge = 56.0, median issue importance = 65.0, median confidence = 74.0 on 0-100 scales; see SI:3), suggesting that our random assignment of propositions did not systematically force writers to opine on issues they felt uninformed about or indifferent toward.

Writers strictly preferred the AI paragraph to their own in a clear majority of cases (2,835 of 4,503 cases, 63.0%), and this preference held across AI models and writer inputs (preference rate >50% across all conditions at p<.01; see SI:4.1).
Results are robust to relaxing both restrictions (see SI:5.2).

Across most dimensions, AI- assisted paragraphs were rated significantly more similarly to each other than their human-written counterparts (significant reduction in standard deviation [scale attributes] or entropy [categorical attributes] for 22 of 29 rating attributes at p<.001 after Bonferroni correction; see SI:5.9).

On nearly every measure, all three models in our study (Claude, DeepSeek, ChatGPT) produced significant distortions in the same direction (18/20 scale attributes and 5/5 ordinal attributes at p<.05; see SI:5.7), and in no case did two models produce significant distortions in opposite directions.

While exact distortion magnitudes varied across models (significant difference in AME for at least one model pair for 14/20 scale attributes and 5/5 ordinal attributes at p<.05; see SI:5.7), no single model was consistently most distortive (avg. abs. AME = 8.4, 8.4, 8.3 for Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek across the 20 scale attributes; see SI:5.7), suggesting that the patterns we observe reflect properties of current AI writing assistance in general rather than the design choices of any one model provider.

They were strongest when models received only a numeric stance rating (avg. abs. AME of 10.2 across the 20 scale attributes; see SI:5.8) or bullet points (9.8), but clearly present even when models received the writer’s full paragraph (5.9 when model was asked to “improve” paragraph, 4.5 when asked to “rewrite”).

We found that these disclaimers had no reliable impact on the tendency of writers to edit the AI-written paragraphs (23.1% edit rate in no-disclaimer control, no disclaimer condition significant, p>.05; see SI:7.3) nor did they change the rate at which writers strictly preferred AI writing to their own (57.8% in no-disclaimer control, no disclaimer condition significant, p>.05; see SI:7.3).
As a first intervention, we tried Prompting: appending a short instruction (113 words; see SI:8.1) to the AI model’s generation prompt, explicitly directing it to preserve the writer’s issue stance.

Perceived writer polarity, for instance, was associated with how confident, clear, and knowledgeable writers appeared (Pearson’s r = 0.60, 0.52, 0.28, all p<.001; full correlation analyses in SI:5.5).

This result replicates for a continuous measure of distortion magnitude (+0.98p Trust Game allocation and +1.47 stance shift per 1 SD increase in distortion from AI writing assistance, both p<.001; see SI:9.4 and SI:10.4).
All studies were preregistered (1: osf.io/6exf2, 2 & 3: osf.io/sf7rg, 4: osf.io/38sg7, 5: osf.io/e48g2).

statements.quote: Following our pre-registration, we include crossed random intercepts for readers, writers, and propositions in the beta regressions for 0-100 scale attributes and in the one-vs-all logistic regressions for nominal attributes described below. Our pre-registration also specified that we would reduce the random-effects structure in case of convergence issues. For the ordinal and multinomial logistic regressions, models with more than one random-effects term were computationally infeasible on our data: cumulative link mixed models with multiple random-effects terms require a general Laplace approximation, which was impractically slow for our 75,972–90,145 observations, and mixed multinomial logistic regressions with multiple random-effects terms, estimated via penalised quasi- likelihood, exceeded available memory or failed. We therefore fit ordinal and multinomial logistic regressions with reader random intercepts only. For most rating attributes, reader random intercepts account for the largest share of variance among the three random effects, and adding writer and proposition random intercepts leaves our estimates essentially unchanged (SI:5.8). Secondary analyses of Study 1 (SI:5.12, SI:5.13, and SI:5.16) use reader random intercepts only.

statements.quote: All differences are significant at p<.001 after Bonferroni correction. Differences point in the same direction for all three AI models, except for paragraph length (DeepSeek V3 paragraphs were 3.2 words shorter than human-written paragraphs on average), with some variation in magnitude. For example, Flesch-Kincaid grade levels ranged from 12.9 (DeepSeek V3) to 15.6 (Claude Sonnet 4), and MTLD from 138.8 (ChatGPT-4o) to 164.9 (Claude Sonnet 4). Across input conditions, AI-written paragraphs contained slightly more errors when the AI model was given the full human-written paragraph to rewrite (0.06 errors per 100 words) or improve (0.07) than when it was given only the writer’s stance (0.02) or bullet points (0.03), consistent with some errors being carried over from the human-written paragraph. Full results by AI model and input condition are available in our code repository.

statements.quote: Our target sample size of 800 analysable readers was determined in advance and pre-registered (osf.io/38sg7). It was based on a simulation-based power analysis under conservative assumptions, primarily driven by the interaction test (whether the AI advantage scales with distortion), since the main effect of paragraph type is well powered at every sample size considered. We simu- lated data under the design described above and fitted the pre-registered models, treating the paragraph_type × distortion_bin interaction as the binding test. Assuming a small AI ad- vantage in the low-distortion bin (8.0p vs. 7.5p average allocation) that widens in the high-distortion bin (8.5p vs. 7.0p), with a between-reader SD of 0.60 on the logit scale and beta precision ϕ = 3, 800 readers yield 84.2% power for the interaction and effectively 100% power for the main effect at α = .05 (for comparison, 600 readers yield 71.8% power for the interaction, and 1,000 readers raise it to 89.6%). 800 is the smallest grid point clearing the conventional 80% threshold on the binding test. The realised sample of 802 analysable readers meets this target.

statements.quote: Our target sample size of 8,000 analysable readers was determined in advance and pre-registered (osf.io/e48g2). As in Study 4, it was based on a simulation-based power analysis under conservative assumptions, primarily driven by the dose-response contrast (whether the AI advantage scales with distortion), which we treated as the binding test since the main effect of paragraph type is well powered at every sample size considered. We simulated data under the design described above and fitted the same crossed reader/proposition models used in our confirmatory analyses (§10.4). We assumed the off-topic control produces no net drift (0 points), a small AI advantage in the low-distortion bin (2.5 vs. 3.0 points of stance shift) that widens in the high-distortion bin (1.0 vs. 3.0 points) – i.e. an average AI-vs.-human effect of 1.25 points and a distortion interaction of 1.5 points on the 0–100 attitude scale – with a between-reader SD of 10 points and within-reader variability partitioned into a between-proposition SD of 6 points and a residual SD of approximately 22 points. Under these assumptions, 8,000 readers yield 87.8% power for the interaction and effectively 100% power for the main effect at α = .05 (for comparison, 6,000 readers yield 74.4% power for the interaction, and 10,000 readers raise it to 92.4%). The larger target than in Study 4 reflects the smaller expected per-observation effect on the 0–100 stance-shift scale and the resulting need for more readers to power the interaction. 8,000 is the smallest grid point clearing the 80% threshold on the binding test with a comfortable margin. The realised sample of 7,996 analysable readers meets this target.

what_we_could_compute: S1 and S3: per-writer averages of originality, clarity, informativeness, relevance and formality, arm means/SDs/SEs, within-writer contrasts, and outcome-specific analyzed writer counts after applying the recorded preference and editing restrictions. The inspected numeric paragraph summaries, text files and proposition responses are fully linked by writer and proposition. These address the open distinct-writer counts and writer-level uncertainty items.

S3: all randomized mitigation contrasts, including originality for None, Prompting and Reranking, with numeric SEs/CIs from reanalysis that preserves within-writer assignment and repeated outputs; reader IDs are also present in the inspected raw rating file. The repository also posts an inspected three-row originality result table with AMEs and confidence bounds. Current published regression precision should not automatically be substituted for writer-level uncertainty.

S1: randomized model/input configuration contrasts and corresponding writer-level summaries from the observed model_name and model_input_condition fields. The pooled human-versus-AI sequence remains nonrandomized, as recorded in the screening form.

S1 and S3: lexical and semantic diversity/homogenization measures from the inspected writer paragraphs, bullet points, model paragraphs and edited paragraphs, grouped by writer, proposition and assigned condition; uncertainty can be recomputed at the appropriate writer/proposition level. Texts and identifiers are present, rather than only precomputed similarity scores.

S1: paragraph- or writer-level numeric dispersion from the inspected mean-rating summaries. The inspected 29-row spread_bootstrap_by_type.csv additionally supplies the published rating-level SD/entropy results and confidence intervals, and the public code reveals the rating-level resampling unit. Exact recomputation of those rating-level distributions, or changing their dependence assumptions, requires the full S1 raw ratings file, which is publicly listed but was not read because it exceeds 20 MB. Modal categorical summaries alone do not recover rating-level entropy.

Initial assignment and attrition totals cannot be reconstructed from the inspected completer CSVs. The newer public supplement reports aggregate attrition funnels in Section 1.5, Tables S17-S21 and surrounding text (pp. 11-14), which can address parts of that open item by extraction rather than participant-level reanalysis. No public participant-level noncompleter/attrition file was confirmed.
